docs.title: Client Communication Standards
docs.text: How we communicate with clients is as important as what we build for them. Sloppy communication erodes trust faster than a missed deadline. These standards exist so every client has a consistent, professional experience regardless of which DM or engineer they're talking to.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
Proactive over reactive. Don't wait for the client to ask for an update. If something changed, something slipped, or something came up — reach out. Clients who feel they have to chase us for information lose confidence fast.

One voice on the account. The Delivery Manager is the primary client contact. Engineers and other team members can communicate directly with client counterparts on day-to-day technical matters, but anything involving scope, timeline, budget, or escalation goes through the DM. Clients should never hear conflicting messages from different people on our team.

Write it down. If a decision is made in a meeting or a call, it gets confirmed in writing — in an email, a status update, or a meeting recap — within 24 hours. Verbal agreements have a short shelf life.

No surprises. A client should never hear bad news for the first time in a weekly report. If something significant is happening, loop them in immediately. The report confirms and summarizes; it doesn't break news.

docs.title: Communication Channels
docs.text:
We use specific channels for specific purposes. Don't blur the lines — using the wrong channel for the wrong message creates confusion and undermines professionalism.

Email is the primary record of client communication. Project status updates, decisions, scope discussions, and anything that needs to be documented goes to email. Response time: within 24 hours during business days, within 4 hours for anything flagged urgent.

Video calls (Zoom or Teams) are for discussions that benefit from real-time dialogue — kickoffs, demos, discovery sessions, and escalations. Every call has an agenda shared in advance and a written recap sent within 24 hours of the call. Never call a meeting for something that can be resolved in an email.

Shared project tools (ADO, Jira, or similar) are for story-level communication — acceptance criteria, technical clarifications, and feedback on specific work items. Client contacts who are in the tool can comment directly on work items. That's appropriate and encouraged for day-to-day collaboration.

Phone or text is reserved for genuine urgency — production down, critical blocker, emergency decision needed. If you're texting or calling a client, something serious is happening. Make sure it actually is.

Do not use Teams DM or informal chat for business-critical communication unless the client has explicitly established that as their preference. Chat is ephemeral and gets lost.

docs.title: Meeting Standards
docs.text:
Every client meeting follows the same discipline:

Agenda in advance. Send the agenda at least 24 hours before the meeting. For recurring ceremonies (sprint demo, backlog refinement), maintain a standing agenda that gets updated each cycle.

Start and end on time. Respect the client's calendar. If the conversation is running long, name it: "We have five minutes left — should we schedule time to finish this?"

Cameras on by default. For video calls with clients, cameras on is the expectation unless the client has indicated otherwise. It signals engagement.

Named next steps. Every meeting ends with a summary of decisions made and next steps, with a named owner and a date for each item. Send the written recap within 24 hours.

No dead air on important items. If a decision was needed and the client hasn't responded, follow up after 48 hours. If it's blocking work, escalate the urgency in your message.

docs.title: Tone and Language
docs.text:
Professional but not stiff. We're a partner, not a vendor. Write and speak like a trusted colleague who happens to be an expert in software delivery.

Plain English. Avoid internal jargon (ADO, sprint poker, DoD, story points) without explanation. When you need to use a technical term, define it briefly in context. Clients shouldn't feel like they need a decoder ring to follow our communications.

Own the situation. When something goes wrong, don't hedge or deflect. "We underestimated the complexity of the integration, and here's what we're doing to correct it" is better than "the timeline was impacted by unforeseen technical factors." One builds trust; the other reads like a press release.

Positive framing is not spin. Be direct about problems — don't bury them in good news. But do lead with context: the client needs to understand what's happening before they can evaluate the impact.

docs.title: Scope and Change Requests
docs.text:
Clients will ask for things that aren't in scope. This is normal. The way we handle it determines whether it creates friction or strengthens the relationship.

When a client requests something outside the SOW:

  1. Acknowledge the request positively — "That makes sense, let me assess the impact."
  2. Don't say yes or no on the spot. Assess the effort and impact first.
  3. Document the request in writing — a quick email confirming what was asked.
  4. Return with a clear answer: in scope, out of scope with a change order estimate, or a suggestion for how to accommodate it within existing scope by de-prioritizing something else.

Never let a scope request disappear. Either it gets acted on or it gets explicitly declined with a reason.

docs.title: Escalation Protocol
docs.text:
When a client is unhappy, escalating it fast is almost always the right move. Trying to manage a frustrated client at the DM level while hiding it from leadership makes things worse.

Signals that it's time to escalate to the Portfolio Manager:

  • A client exec has expressed dissatisfaction directly or via their PM
  • The client has asked for a DM change
  • A formal complaint has been received
  • The client is unresponsive for more than a week without explanation
  • You're in a standoff over scope or budget that isn't moving

The Portfolio Manager can de-escalate conversations that have become adversarial at the DM level. Involve them early, not as a last resort.

docs.title: Client Onboarding to Tools
docs.text:
When a client needs access to shared tools (ADO boards, Notion pages, SharePoint folders), the DM is responsible for provisioning access and walking the client through what they'll see and how to use it.

First-time access always comes with a short orientation — either a 15-minute video call or a written guide, depending on client preference. Don't just throw a link at them and assume they'll figure it out.

docs.title: Offboarding and Relationship Close
docs.text:
When an engagement ends, the DM conducts a formal closeout conversation with the client (see Project Lifecycle). Even if the client relationship is ending, leave cleanly — archived documentation, transferred access, and a genuine conversation about what went well and what could have been better.

How we end engagements affects whether clients refer us to others and whether they come back.

docs.title: How We Work
docs.text: This page describes our operating norms — how we make decisions, communicate, run projects, and improve over time. It's written for anyone joining the team or trying to understand how we operate day to day.

docs.title: Decision-Making
docs.text:
We operate on autonomy with accountability. Each leader and team member owns decisions within their domain and is accountable for the outcomes. The expectation is to act — not to seek permission at every turn.

A few principles that guide how we decide:

Don't escalate decisions — escalate conflicts. If a decision falls within your domain, make it. If it genuinely crosses into another domain, align with that owner. Only escalate when alignment fails.

Disagree and commit. We debate openly and assume good intent. Once a decision is made, everyone commits — even those who argued the other side. Relitigating settled decisions erodes trust and momentum.

Oppose with a proposal. If you challenge an idea, come with an alternative. "That won't work" isn't a contribution. "That won't work, and here's what I'd do instead" is.

Document divergence. If you make a decision that deviates from established practice, write down why. Patterns of undocumented divergence mean the documented approach needs updating.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
We keep communication lean and purposeful. The goal is clarity and speed, not volume.

Channels: - Teams — quick questions, status updates, FYIs. Expected response within a few hours during working hours. - Email — formal communication, client-facing content, documentation. Respond within 24 hours. - Meeting — real-time discussion, decisions, unblocking. Scheduled in advance with an agenda. - ADO — story-specific discussion, technical detail, async decisions on work items. - Phone/video (urgent) — blockers, critical issues, escalations. Immediate during working hours.

After hours: Not expected. If something is genuinely urgent, call or text — not Slack or email.

Meeting norms: Start on time, end on time. Come prepared. Cameras on by default. Close distractions. Every meeting ends with clear next steps and named owners. If a meeting doesn't need to happen, cancel it — a well-written message is often better.

docs.title: How We Run Projects
docs.text:
We use Practical Agile — structured enough to maintain predictability and quality, flexible enough to adapt to client realities. We don't run identical ceremonies on every engagement, but we hold to the underlying discipline.

The baseline on every project: - A defined sprint cadence (typically two weeks) - A sprint goal, agreed at planning - A daily standup: what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me - A demo at sprint end — only completed work, in a production-like environment - A retrospective — internal, psychologically safe, focused on process not people - A backlog kept groomed and ready

Definition of Ready: A story enters a sprint only when acceptance criteria are clear and testable, it's estimated, and dependencies are resolved. We don't pull half-formed work into sprints.

Definition of Done: Code reviewed and approved, tests passing, QA complete, deployed to staging, Product Owner accepted. Done means done — not "mostly done" or "waiting on review."

docs.title: How We Handle Conflict
docs.text:
Conflict is a sign the team is engaging. Avoidance is the real problem.

Step 1 — Go direct. Address the issue with the person involved. Assume positive intent. Focus on behavior and impact, not character. Use "I" statements.

Step 2 — Bring in a mediator. If a direct conversation doesn't resolve it, involve a delivery manager or team lead to facilitate — not to decide, but to help both parties reach understanding.

Step 3 — Escalate. If still unresolved, escalate to the portfolio manager or VP of Delivery for formal resolution.

What's not okay: passive-aggressive behavior, talking behind someone's back, personal attacks, or ignoring the issue and hoping it disappears.

docs.title: How We Improve
docs.text:
We treat our processes the same way we treat software — ship, learn, iterate.

Every project team holds retrospectives. Every quarter, delivery and engineering leadership review the operating model. When something isn't working, we name it, document the change, and move on. We don't preserve bad processes out of habit.

This handbook is a living document. If something here conflicts with how work is actually happening — and that divergence is intentional — update the handbook. If the divergence isn't intentional, fix the practice.

Anyone on the team can propose a change. The standard is: bring a proposal, not just a complaint.

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: We help organizations build better software by delivering with clarity, care, and craft. We don't just ship code — we take responsibility for outcomes.

docs.title: Our Values
docs.text: These aren't aspirations. They're how we make decisions, how we treat each other, and what we're willing to sacrifice to get right.

docs.title: Bias Toward Action
docs.text:
We move. We don't wait for the perfect plan, the complete map, or unanimous consensus. We gather enough information to act intelligently, then we act — and we adjust as we learn. A mediocre decision made now beats a brilliant one made too late.

Procrastination often disguises itself as preparation. When in doubt, ship something, learn something, fix something.

docs.title: Multiply Others
docs.text:
Our job is to make the people around us more capable — not to be the hero who saves the day. Every time someone on our team "just handles it themselves" instead of enabling someone else, we've made the team smaller. Leadership means your output is other people's growth.

We delegate not because we're too busy, but because it's the right model. If someone else can do 80% as well, someone else should.

docs.title: Build the Machine
docs.text:
Professionals build systems. Heroes burn out. We design repeatable, scalable ways of working so that quality doesn't depend on any one person being in the room. If a process relies on tribal knowledge, heroics, or a single point of failure — we fix the process.

This applies to client delivery, internal operations, and how we onboard and develop our people.

docs.title: Integrity Is Expensive
docs.text:
Real values cost something. If a principle only holds when it's easy, it's not a principle — it's a preference. We have the hard conversations, make the difficult calls, and tell clients what they need to hear rather than what they want to hear.

We don't confuse being nice with being kind. Withholding honest feedback to avoid discomfort is a failure of care, not an act of it.

docs.title: Show Up Fully
docs.text:
Presence is respect. Whether it's a client meeting, a team standup, or a 1:1 — we're there. Half-attention is worse than absence because it creates the illusion of engagement without the substance of it.

This extends beyond meetings. When we take on a project, we take it on fully. We don't phone it in.

docs.title: Recognize the Win
docs.text:
Recognition is cultural oxygen. We celebrate progress — loudly, publicly, and without waiting for the perfect moment. A 60-second callout of someone's great work generates more momentum than any all-hands presentation.

We share credit broadly. We amplify others. We make it clear when something went well and who made it happen.

docs.title: What We're Not
docs.text:
Values also mean knowing what we won't tolerate:

Blame without ownership. If something went wrong, we own our part and focus on fixing it, not explaining why it wasn't our fault.

Busy as a badge. Activity isn't the same as impact. We measure what matters, not what's visible.

Silence as politeness. Saying nothing when something needs to be said is a failure of responsibility, not a virtue.

docs.title: Project Manager Responsibilities
docs.text: Owner: Isaac Welch, VP of Delivery Last updated: May 2026 Audience: All project managers and VP of Deliverys

docs.title: The Role
docs.text:
The project manager is the single-threaded owner of a client engagement. Not the coordinator. Not the facilitator. The owner. That means one person is accountable for whether the project ships on time, on budget, and to functional quality — and one person the client can call when something goes wrong. The PM treats their engagement like a mini-business: they understand the budget, know where it's going, and are responsible for the outcome.

This document defines what that ownership looks like — the accountabilities, the boundaries, the working relationships, the decision rights, and how performance is measured. For how to perform the behaviors inside this role, read the PM Standards Playbook. For what to do at each phase of an engagement, read the Project Lifecycle. This document is about what you own.

docs.title: Why This Role Is Designed This Way
docs.text:
Most project management failures are not planning failures. They are leadership failures: someone who knew about a problem but waited, someone who managed tasks instead of outcomes, someone who confused activity with accountability.

This role is designed around three ideas that directly address those failures.

The PM's job is to create conditions, not to be the solver. The best delivery teams we've worked with had one thing in common: the PM shaped the problem clearly, handed it to the team, and then got out of the way. From 37signals:

give teams a fixed time and a well-defined problem, then trust them to find the solution. ~37Signals When a PM starts solving the problem themselves, it's usually a sign they haven't trusted the team — or haven't equipped them well enough to trust. Either way, the fix is leadership, not heroics. "Your job is not to solve every problem, but your job is to ensure every problem gets solved." ~Pam Butkowski

A PM who only hears good news hasn't built safety — they've built silence. A PM's job is to create the conditions where the team surfaces problems early, not after they've become recoverable — or not. That means running retros that aren't performances, asking hard questions in 1:1s, and making it clear that a problem raised early is valued more than a problem hidden until it explodes. If you want to know your project's true health, measure how fast your team brings you bad news.

PM competence has three layers, and all three matter. The PMI's competency framework identifies three dimensions: what you know, how you apply it, and how you behave. A PM who can recite the PMBOK but freezes when a client escalates is incomplete. A PM who runs perfect ceremonies but hoards information and manages up rather than out is incomplete. The job requires all three — knowledge of the craft, consistent execution, and the personal maturity to hold the line when it's uncomfortable.

The underlying principle across all of it: empathy earns the right to demand excellence. Clear expectations are respect, not cruelty. The PM who sets a vague goal and then holds someone accountable to it has failed their team. The PM who sets a precise standard and enforces it honestly has given the team something to aim at. Systems beat heroics. One PM grinding through chaos is not a delivery model — it's a liability.

docs.title: 1. Engagement P&L Ownership
docs.text:
The PM owns the financial health of their engagement. This is not optional or secondary — it is a core accountability, not a number tracked by finance.

  • Know the SOW: total budget, billing model, margin target, milestone structure
  • Track burn rate weekly — hours logged vs. hours planned; flag variance before it becomes an overrun
  • Manage scope as the primary financial tool: when the engagement is trending over, scope is the first lever, not schedule
  • Document, price, and secure approval for every scope change before any work begins — no verbal yeses
  • Own the margin narrative: be able to speak to the engagement's financial health at any check-in without being asked
  • Know the receivables status before agreeing to any scope increase. The PM doesn't collect — but doesn't expand scope on an account that isn't current.
  • Surface renewal and expansion signals to the VP of Delivery — a closed engagement with no next step is a missed opportunity

docs.title: 2. Client Relationship Management
docs.text:
The PM is the client's primary contact. Not the engineer they trust most. Not the VP of Delivery on escalation. The PM — consistently, reliably, and proactively.

  • Map stakeholders by influence and interest at project start — not every client contact needs the same update
  • Communicate before the client asks; never deliver news they discover on their own
  • Run weekly written status updates in the client's preferred channel — Smart Brevity format, every Friday without exception
  • Send meeting recaps within 24 hours: decisions, action items, owners, due dates
  • Deliver bad news with a plan — not alone, not passively, not buried in a paragraph of positives
  • Hold the scope line professionally: "Can we just add this?" gets a process, not a yes
  • Treat a disengaged stakeholder as a risk — if a key decision-maker goes quiet, that's a problem to solve, not a gift
  • Identify satisfaction signals (positive and negative) and surface them to the VP of Delivery

docs.title: 3. Team Leadership & Scrum Facilitation
docs.text:
The PM leads the delivery team day-to-day. That means running the ceremonies, removing blockers, creating psychological safety, and holding the team to its commitments — without micromanaging how the work gets done.

  • Run every sprint ceremony on schedule: planning, daily standup, backlog refinement, review, retrospective
  • Remove blockers within 24 hours — if something is in the team's way, name it and move it
  • Make blockers visible immediately; don't let anything sit in a queue waiting for a weekly meeting
  • Create safety for the team to raise concerns, flag risks, and ask for help — if you're only hearing good news, dig
  • Hold the team to sprint commitments without controlling the path — give the problem, trust the solution
  • Maintain a healthy, well-groomed backlog in partnership with the engineering & product teams: 2+ sprints of Ready work at all times
  • Partner with the Tech Lead on quality and technical concerns that surface within the engagement
  • Establish team norms, decision rights, and escalation paths at kickoff — not after the first conflict
  • Set the board discipline at kickoff: engineers own their own tickets. ADO reflects the team's real work, not the PM's summary of it. If a ticket isn't updated, that's a standup conversation — not a task the PM absorbs
  • If it isn't in ADO, it didn't happen. A story that exists only in someone's head or in a Teams chat does not exist

docs.title: 4. Scope & Delivery Management
docs.text:
The PM owns the engagement's statement of work, the milestone plan, and the risk register. These are not documents that get created at kickoff and filed — they are live instruments that drive weekly decisions.

  • Track progress against plan weekly; maintain an honest, current picture of status at all times
  • Update the risk register weekly — top three risks always visible, with owner and mitigation
  • Run a pre-mortem before every high-stakes phase — required for all engagements >$100k; complete it before the phase begins and file the output
  • Distinguish between risk (known unknowns you can plan for) and ambiguity (unknown unknowns requiring exploratory action) — they need different responses
  • When ambiguity is high, propose a discovery phase or technical spike before committing to a fixed-price delivery; a spike converts ambiguity into information, a fixed-price commitment converts it into margin risk
  • Assess every scope change request for effort, timeline, and budget impact before responding
  • Use the scope change memo template for every change, regardless of size — pattern recognition depends on it
  • Coordinate dependencies across teams, vendors, and client stakeholders that affect delivery
  • Build schedule and budget contingency explicitly — hidden padding is not a risk strategy

docs.title: 5. Information Stewardship
docs.text:
The PM is the librarian of the engagement. Information lives in one place per type, it's current, and anyone who needs it can find it without asking.

  • New meeting → meeting note within 24 hours, with action items linked to the task tracker
  • New client touchpoint (call, key email, decision) → INTERACTION logged in project tracker
  • New deliverable → SharePoint, in the right client folder
  • New work item → ADO, sized and labeled
  • Every decision captured in writing — if it's worth making, it's worth recording
  • Every action item has one owner, not "we" or "the team"
  • Nothing critical lives only in a Teams chat

docs.title: 6. Reporting & Escalation
docs.text:
The VP of Delivery should be able to assess the health of any engagement at any time without asking. The PM makes that possible by keeping records current and escalating before problems become crises.

  • Deliver weekly engagement status to the VP of Delivery by Friday EOD — every week, without exception
  • Format: situation, impact, what you're doing, what you need
  • Escalate within 24 hours when any threshold is crossed (see Decision Authority section below)
  • Maintain clean, current records at all times
  • Hold the team accountable for keeping Azure DevOps current — the PM enforces ADO discipline, not performs it; an out-of-date board is a team behavior problem, not a PM to-do item
  • Flag scope creep, client friction, and team issues early — never after they've become visible to others

docs.title: What This Role Is Not
docs.text:
Not an individual contributor who also manages. When a PM is doing too much hands-on technical or design work, the engagement is either understaffed or the PM hasn't fully stepped into the ownership mindset. Leadership is the job. Execution is what the team does.

Not the technical decision-maker. The Tech Lead owns architecture, development standards, and technical implementation choices. The PM is accountable for the outcome of technical work — not the method by which it's produced. When a PM starts overriding technical judgment, they've left their lane. When technical quality threatens the engagement, the PM's job is to surface it to the Tech Lead and VP of Technology — not to solve it.

Quality accountability is split, not shared. The PM is accountable for functional quality: does this feature solve the client's stated problem? Do the acceptance criteria capture the right requirement? Is what was built what was asked for? That is the PM's standard to hold. Structural quality — code health, test coverage standards, architecture soundness, bug severity at the implementation level — belongs to the Tech Lead. When structural quality threatens the engagement, the PM escalates. When functional quality is at risk, the PM owns the fix. On engagements where a Product Owner is present, functional quality ownership transfers to that role. The PM's accountability then shifts to ensuring the PO has the information, access, and authority to exercise it.

Not the VP of Delivery. Cross-engagement resourcing, agency pricing strategy, client executive relationships, and new contract decisions belong to the VP of Delivery. A PM who escalates everything upward isn't owning the engagement. A PM who never escalates isn't either. The boundary is clear: own what's yours, escalate what isn't.

docs.title: Daily
docs.text:
• Review overnight client communications and flag anything requiring same-day response
  • Run the daily standup (15 minutes, no more)
  • Resolve or escalate blockers surfaced in standup before they affect today's work
  • Keep ADO current — stories reflect actual status, blockers are visible, work in progress is accurate

docs.title: Weekly
docs.text:
• Deliver internal status update to VP of Delivery by Friday EOD
  • Deliver client-facing written status update in the client's preferred channel
  • Update the risk register — top three risks with owner and mitigation
  • Review budget burn: hours logged vs. planned, flag any trend before it becomes a variance
  • Clear all pending action items or explicitly reassign with updated dates
  • Confirm backlog has at least 2 sprints of Ready work

docs.title: Sprint
docs.text:
• Sprint planning: confirm sprint goal, validate all entering stories meet Definition of Ready, commit as a team
  • Mid-sprint refinement: groom upcoming stories, add acceptance criteria and estimates
  • Sprint review: demo completed work to client against acceptance criteria — only stories that meet Definition of Done
  • Retrospective: run internally with no client present, capture 1–2 action items with owners
  • Burndown reviewed and archived; sprint notes captured in MEETINGS

docs.title: Monthly
docs.text:
• Margin and health review with VP of Delivery — budget vs. actual, velocity trend, risk summary
  • Billable utilization reviewed via ATP export
  • Progress against engagement milestone plan confirmed or formally renegotiated

docs.title: Quarterly
docs.text:
• Client Business Review — formal session with client stakeholders covering value delivered, roadmap alignment, relationship health
  • Engagement forecast updated: remaining budget, projected completion, scope and staffing risks

docs.title: Working Relationships
docs.text:
Relationship Nature Key interface PMO Lead Direct manager Weekly 1:1, status report, escalation path for budget/client/resource decisions above PM authority Tech Lead Peer Structural quality (code health, test coverage, architecture) and implementation choices — PM owns functional quality and acceptance; Tech Lead owns structural quality and method Delivery Team Day-to-day direct leadership Ceremonies, blockers, sprint commitment, psychological safety Client Stakeholders Primary relationship owner Weekly status, sprint demo, scope and decision conversations — the PM is the client's first call Other PMs Peers Knowledge-sharing, lessons learned, cross-engagement dependencies surfaced upward

The PM is not the escalation path for technical architecture decisions. The PM is not the person who manages cross-engagement capacity. The PM is the person who owns everything inside the engagement.

docs.title: Decision Authority
docs.text:
The PM acts without escalation on:

Domain PM decides Budget Reallocate hours within sprint; adjust team composition within budget; defer non-critical work to manage burn Timeline Sprint schedule within release timeline; internal milestone adjustments; velocity-based forecasting Scope Story breakdown and acceptance criteria; technical implementation details; minor clarifications of existing requirements (<5% effort impact); story priority within sprint Functional Quality Whether acceptance criteria are met; whether delivered work solves the client's stated problem; when to demo to the client; bug priority relative to client impact Resources Daily task assignments; sprint team composition; coverage during PTO; request for specialist support Client Day-to-day communication; status report frequency and format; demo schedule and content; working session attendees

The PM escalates to VP of Delivery within the stated response time when:

Trigger Response time Production outage, security incident, client threatening contract termination 4 hours Budget variance >10% or >$25K; timeline at risk; client satisfaction issue; key team member departure 24 hours Client 30+ days past due on any invoice, or scope expansion requested on an account with aged receivables 24 hours Scope change request >10% of effort; resource addition needed 3 business days Scope change <10%; minor process adjustment Next scheduled check-in

docs.title: How We Measure Performance
docs.text: Metric Target Measured by Project margin ≥60% Revenue – Cost / Revenue Billable utilization ≥75% Billable hours / total capacity Budget variance ±10% Actual hours vs. estimated at engagement close Client satisfaction ≥4.5/5 Post-sprint survey scores Velocity stability ±15% sprint-over-sprint Sprint tracking On-time milestone delivery ≥90% Milestones within ±1 week

docs.title: What strong performance looks like
docs.text:
Systems thinker. Builds repeatable processes, not one-off solutions. Documents decisions and learnings for future engagements. Proactively identifies and fixes broken workflows before they become the next project's problem.

Proactive communicator. Surfaces issues early — not when they've become crises. Provides context, not just status. Tailors communication to audience without losing directness.

Margin-conscious. Understands the business model. Makes trade-off decisions that protect profitability. Negotiates scope changes that preserve margin, not just client relationships.

Client advocate and company representative. Balances client needs with company constraints. Says no when necessary, with alternatives. Builds long-term trust by being honest about trade-offs rather than agreeable about everything.

Calm under pressure. Doesn't panic when projects hit turbulence. Breaks large problems into manageable decisions. Maintains team confidence and client trust during the hard stretches — which every project has.

docs.title: The Five Standards
docs.text:
1. Status Visibility — No surprises. Weekly written update in Notion every Friday. Health changes get a Teams message within 24h.
  2. Information Stewardship — One place per type. Meetings in Notion, work in ADO, files in SharePoint, decisions logged.
  3. Client Communication — Weekly written update to client. Recaps within 24h. Bad news with a plan, before they ask.
  4. Scope & Risk Management — Risk register weekly. Scope changes via memo with impact + recommendation. No verbal yeses.
  5. Delivery Discipline — Run the ceremonies. Watch the margins. End engagements cleanly.

docs.text:
• Daily — ADO updates current
  • Weekly Friday — status to Isaac and client
  • Sprint — planning, review, retro
  • Monthly — margin + health review

  • Margin within 5 points of target

  • Resource constraint affects delivery
  • Scope change request >10% of effort

docs.title: Playbook — What I expect from every project manager
docs.text:
Owner: Isaac Welch, VP of Delivery Last updated: May 8, 2026 Audience: All project managers

Related: PM Responsibilities — what the role owns, its boundaries, decision authority, and how performance is measured. This playbook covers the behavioral standards inside that role.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Project managers are the operating system of every engagement. When Project Managers (PM) run well, clients feel confident, teams stay focused, and engagements stay healthy. When they don't, the symptoms show up everywhere: surprise status updates, missed risks, scattered information, scope creep, eroded margins.

This document lays out what I expect from every PM. It is not a rigid script. It is the set of principles, behaviors, and standards that define how we operate as a delivery agency. Use the templates and examples to adapt to your client's context, but hold the core standards as non-negotiable.

The five standards below answer one question: how do we deliver software for clients without surprises?

docs.title: 1. Status Visibility
docs.text:
Principle: I should never be surprised by a project's status. Surface issues before they become recoveries.

What this looks like:

  • A weekly written status update lives in the document repository every Friday by EOD, regardless of whether I asked.
  • The PROJECTS database always reflects current state — health (Green / Yellow / Red), % complete, % timeline burned, current sprint, top risks.
  • If health changes from green to yellow or yellow to red, I get a Teams message within 24 hours of the change. Don't wait for the weekly update.
  • "We thought we'd catch up next sprint" is not a status update. If you're behind, say it the day you know.
  • Track 3-5 leading indicators per project — metrics that predict delivery health, not just confirm it after the fact. Velocity trends, blocked item count, and acceptance rate are more useful than % complete alone.
  • Metrics are for the team, not just leadership. If the team can't see the numbers, the numbers won't change behavior.
  • Act on variance immediately. A metric that doesn't change a decision isn't worth tracking.

Examples:

  • Good: "VFW Command Post slipped from 65% to 58% complete this sprint. Root cause: discovery on the auth integration revealed a third-party API limitation. Revised plan and 2-week impact attached."
  • Weak: "Sprint went well overall, working through some blockers, will update next week."

docs.title: 2. Information Stewardship
docs.text:
Principle: Information lives in one place per type. PMs are the librarians.

What this looks like:

  • New meeting → MEETING note within 24 hours, with action items linked to task tracker.
  • New client touchpoint (call, important email, decision) → INTERACTION documented.
  • New deliverable → SharePoint, in the right client folder (/Clients/[Client]/[Project]/).
  • New work item → ADO, sized, labeled.
  • Decision made → captured in the project's NOTES or in the relevant meeting record. If it's worth remembering, it's worth writing down.
  • Every action item has one owner — not a team, not "we." Ambiguous ownership means it won't get done.
  • Blockers are cleared within 24 hours or escalated. Nothing sits. If it's in your way, name it and move it.

Examples:

  • Good: Client emails about a scope change → reply, log INTERACTION, create TASK or ADO ticket, update PROJECTS health if material.
  • Weak: Decision made on a Teams call, lives only in chat history.

docs.title: 3. Client Communication
docs.text:
Principle: Be ahead of the client. Direct, structured, no fluff.

What this looks like:

  • Every client gets a weekly written update in their preferred channel (default: email, Smart Brevity format).
  • Every meeting has a recap within 24 hours: decisions, action items, owners, due dates.
  • Bad news is delivered before the client asks. Always with the plan.
  • Pushback is part of the job. If a client decision puts the engagement at risk, surface it directly — not in a passive footnote.
  • Map stakeholders by influence and interest at project start. Not every stakeholder needs the same update — tailor format and frequency to their role.
  • Treat disengaged stakeholders as a risk. If a key decision-maker goes quiet, that is a problem to solve, not a gift.
  • Deliver incrementally where the engagement allows. Don't hold value until the end. Early wins build trust; surprises at delivery erode it.

Examples:

  • Good: "Three updates this week: sprint goal hit (auth flow shipped to staging), one risk emerging (data migration timing tight for Phase 2), one decision needed (final UX review by Thursday). Details below."
  • Weak: "Hi team, hope you're well! Just wanted to circle back and share some updates from the past week…"

docs.title: 4. Scope & Risk Management
docs.text:
Principle: Scope and risk are PM jobs. Don't outsource them to the client or the engineering team.

What this looks like:

  • A risk register lives in the project's files, updated weekly. Top three risks always visible, with owner and mitigation.
  • Scope changes are documented. Use the scope change memo template. Quantify impact (effort, timeline, budget). Get a written decision before any work starts.
  • "Can we just add…" gets a process, not a yes. Even small additions go through the memo. Pattern recognition matters.
  • Risks are surfaced with options, not as problems. Bring the trade-off, not the panic.
  • Distinguish between risk (known unknowns you can plan for) and ambiguity (unknown unknowns requiring exploratory action). They require different responses — don't treat them the same way.
  • When ambiguity is high, your accountability is to name it and sell the client on a discovery phase or technical spike — a short, time-boxed effort (typically 1–2 sprints) with a defined output and fixed cost — rather than committing to a fixed-price delivery you can't yet defend. A spike converts ambiguity into information. A fixed-price commitment on ambiguous scope converts ambiguity into margin risk.
  • Build schedule and budget contingency explicitly. Hidden padding is not a risk strategy; it just delays the conversation.
  • Run a pre-mortem before every high-stakes phase. Ask: "if this phase fails, what killed it?" Surface assumptions before they become failures. Required for all engagements >$100k — see Mandatory Gates below.

Examples:

  • Good: "Client requested feature X mid-sprint. Effort ~3 days. Trade-off options: (A) defer feature Y to next sprint, (B) extend sprint by 3 days, (C) absorb risk and recommend in Phase 2. Recommendation: B. Awaiting client decision."
  • Weak: "Client wants X, I told them yes, we'll figure it out."

docs.title: 5. Delivery Discipline
docs.text:
Principle: Run the ceremonies. Watch the margins. Hit the bar.

What this looks like:

  • Sprint planning, review, and retro happen on schedule. No exceptions.
  • The board is the source of truth. Engineers update their own tickets. The PM's job is to enforce the standard — not to be the data entry. A sprint board that only stays current because the PM is updating it isn't a board; it's the PM's opinion of the work.
  • Definition of Done is applied consistently. Code reviewed, tested, deployed, demoed, documented.
  • Margins reviewed monthly via ATP export and the KPI report. PM owns the conversation if a project is below margin target.
  • Engagements end cleanly. Final deliverable, retrospective, lessons learned in NOTES, formal handoff or closeout.
  • Establish team norms, decision rights, and escalation paths at kickoff — not after the first conflict. Teams that know how they work together outperform teams that figure it out under pressure.
  • Create psychological safety. Teams that surface problems early outperform teams that hide them. If your team is only bringing you good news, something is wrong.
  • Match authority to accountability. Don't hold people responsible for outcomes they can't influence.
  • Choose delivery methodology — waterfall, agile, or hybrid — based on requirements stability and delivery risk, not habit or client preference. Get stakeholder alignment on the approach before work begins. Revisit it at phase transitions.
  • Plan to the level of detail you can actually defend. Use rolling wave planning: detail the near term, keep the horizon directional. A plan that never changes isn't being used.

docs.title: Source of Truth Map
docs.text:
One place per type of information. The recommendation below is what every PM should default to.

Type of information Lives in Why Project record (status, health, scope, % complete) PROJECTS Single executive view Engineering work (epics, stories, bugs, tasks) Azure DevOps Sprint execution and team velocity Meeting notes MEETINGS Searchable and linkable Client touchpoints (calls, decisions, escalations) INTERACTIONS Relationship history Files, deliverables, contracts SharePoint /Clients/[Client]/ Formal artifacts Time and utilization ATP* → KPI report Margin and capacity Client email Outlook (key items logged in INTERACTIONS) External channel of record Internal team comms Teams Day-to-day coordination only

* ATP time tracking to be replaced with alternative tool.

Rule of thumb: if two people might need it later, it doesn't live in a Teams chat.

docs.title: Communication Cadence
docs.text:
The minimum cadence below applies to every engagement. You can add more, never less. Adjust client-facing rhythm to match the engagement, but never drop below weekly.

Cadence What Where Daily ADO updates current; blockers visible ADO + Teams Weekly (Friday EOD) Internal status update PROJECTS + email to Isaac & Jason Weekly Client status update Email, Smart Brevity format Sprint Planning, Review, Retro Zoom + MEETINGS Monthly Margin and health review KPI report + 1:1 with Isaac & Jason Quarterly Client Business Review (QBR) In person or Zoom

docs.title: Escalation Triggers
docs.text:
Don't wait for a weekly update. Send a Teams message within 24 hours when any of these occur:

  • Project >10% over timeline OR progress <80% of planned
  • Margin within 5 points of target threshold
  • Client escalates to anyone above the PM (CEO, partner, executive sponsor)
  • Resource constraint will affect delivery (illness, departure, capacity)
  • Scope change request >10% of total effort
  • Trust event — a moment that could affect the client relationship, positive or negative
  • Client is 30+ days past due on any invoice — escalate before approving any scope expansion or renewal commitment

Format: situation, impact, what you're doing about it, what you need from me.

docs.title: Mandatory Gates
docs.text: The following are not best practices — they are required steps. They apply automatically when the threshold is met. A PM cannot waive them; escalation to the Portfolio Manager is required if they cannot be completed before the gate deadline.

docs.title: Pre-Mortem
docs.text:
Applies to: All engagements with total contract value >$100k, and any engagement where a phase carries material delivery or client risk regardless of size.

When: Before the start of any high-stakes phase (project kickoff, major release, go-live). Must be completed before the phase begins — not during it.

What it must produce:

  • A written list of the top failure modes the team identified
  • Owner and mitigation assigned to each
  • Output filed in the project's NOTES before phase work starts

Format: A facilitated session with the delivery team (1 hour). Prompt: "If this phase fails six months from now, what killed it?" Go around the room. Write everything down. Assign owners before you leave.

Who runs it: The PM.

What disqualifies it: A quick chat on a standup call. An async Slack thread. A list the PM wrote alone. The session requires the team's input — individual assumptions are the point.

docs.title: A user story is done when
docs.text:
• Acceptance criteria met
  • Code reviewed and merged
  • Tests passing (unit and integration)
  • Deployed to staging and QA approved
  • Demoed to client (if client-facing)
  • Documentation updated

docs.title: A sprint is done when
docs.text:
• Sprint goal achieved or formally renegotiated
  • Burndown reflected in tracker
  • Review completed with client
  • Retro completed with team
  • Notes captured in MEETINGS

docs.title: A project is done when
docs.text:
• All committed deliverables shipped
  • Client signoff documented in INTERACTIONS
  • Final deliverables filed in SharePoint
  • Retrospective completed
  • Lessons learned captured in NOTES
  • Formal handoff or closeout email sent
  • ATP and KPI updated

docs.title: Onboarding Checklist
docs.text: For new PMs joining the practice, the first 90 days follow this arc.

docs.title: First 30 days
docs.text:
• Shadow one full sprint cycle on a steady-state project
  • Read every active project record in database
  • Meet every client stakeholder on assigned engagements
  • Review the last 90 days of INTERACTIONS for assigned clients
  • Set up ADO, ATP, and SharePoint access; verify everything works

docs.title: First 60 days
docs.text:
• Run a sprint review and retro independently
  • Write a weekly status update Isaac doesn't need to revise
  • Submit first scope change memo (real or simulated)
  • Complete first monthly margin review for assigned project

docs.title: First 90 days
docs.text:
• Own a project end-to-end through one major milestone
  • Lead a client status meeting with no Isaac safety net
  • Identify and surface a real risk before it became visible to others
  • Submit one improvement to PM standards (this document evolves)

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Start from the templates below. They live in /Users/isaac/Documents/_Templates/PM/ — see Isaac if any are missing.

  • Weekly status update — Smart Brevity format
  • Scope change memo — effort, trade-offs, recommendation
  • Risk register — Notion template
  • Project closeout — checklist + email template
  • Meeting recap — Notion MEETINGS

docs.text:
